Population & material context: Foraging bands of ~25–50; world population perhaps <1–5 M, egalitarian, no surplus, no state, no priesthood. Cave art (Chauvet ~36k, Lascaux ~17k), ritual burial with grave goods. Religion = part-time shamanic specialists.

Concept of God: Animism: spirits in animals, weather, places; ancestor spirits; totemism; in some cultures a diffuse "sky/high god." No sovereign personal creator.

Mediator: The shaman — ecstatic soul-flight between worlds; healer and psychopomp.

Cosmos & afterlife: Layered cosmos on an axis mundi / world-tree (upper–middle–lower). Death = passage to a spirit/ancestor realm; cyclical, not morally sorted.

Population & material context: Agriculture, sedentism, surplus, property, rising density. World ~5 → 14 M+. Çatalhöyük ~5–8k people; Göbekli Tepe (c. 9600 BCE) — a monumental temple before farming. Incipient hierarchy.

Concept of God: Fertility powers, horned/bull gods, mother-goddess figurines, ancestor cult (skull caches at Jericho); the contested "Great Goddess." Storm/sky gods emerging.

Mediator: Emerging shrine-tending priest-figures tied to megaliths and temples.

Cosmos & afterlife: Sacred mountain / temple as cosmic center crystallizes. Ancestor veneration; secondary burial.
Reconstructed Indo-European daylight-sky father; reflected in names such as Greek Zeus, Latin Jupiter, and Vedic Dyaus Pitar.
Reconstructed thunder/storm figure often compared with Perun, Perkūnas, Thor, and sometimes Indra.
Reconstructed primordial twin associated with sacrifice/death and cosmic order in the Manu–Yemo complex.
Reconstructed first man/ritual actor paired with Yemo in the cosmogonic sacrifice complex.
Reconstructed Indo-European horse-associated twin rescuers, reflected in the Ashvins, Dioscuri, Baltic Ašvieniai, and related traditions.
Reconstructed dawn goddess reflected by Vedic Ushas, Greek Eos, Latin Aurora, and others.
Reconstructed PIE solar deity/personification; reflected in Vedic Surya, Norse Sól, Greek Helios, Lithuanian Saulė.
Reconstructed PIE fire deity; reflected directly in Vedic Agni and Latin ignis (word level).
Reconstructed PIE concept of fate as spinning a thread; reflected in Norse Norns, Greek Moirai, Roman Parcae.
Reconstructed earth-mother figure; reflected in Vedic Pṛthvī Mātā, Greek Gaia/Demeter complex, Slavic Mat Zemlya.

Reconstructed PIE myth of a hero (often the thunder god) slaying a serpent/dragon and freeing cattle/waters; reflected in Indra vs Vritra, Thor vs Jörmungandr, Zeus vs Typhon, Apollo vs Python, Tarhunna vs Illuyanka.
Reconstructed PIE chthonic deity associated with cattle and the underworld; reflected in Slavic Veles and Baltic Velnias.
Reconstructed PIE cosmogony in which Manu kills Yemo as a foundational sacrifice; widely accepted among comparativists (Lincoln, Puhvel, Mallory & Adams, West, Anthony).
Reconstructed First Warrior who recovers divine cattle stolen by serpent Ngʷhi, aided by the storm-god; establishes the warrior function in Dumézilian readings.
Reconstructed three-headed serpent adversary in the Trito myth; name related to the PIE root for negation (ne-).
Reconstructed pastoral motif of a primordial cow whose milk or sacrifice generates life; best preserved in Indo-Iranian reflexes (Auðumbla, Gōšūrvan); Roman she-wolf serves a reduced nurturing role.
First civilization, invented cuneiform writing and the wheel.
First civilization, invented cuneiform writing and the wheel
Cradle of civilization in the Fertile Crescent
Advanced urban civilization with sophisticated city planning and drainage systems.
Advanced urban civilization with sophisticated city planning and drainage systems
One of the world's oldest civilizations, known for pyramids, hieroglyphs, and pharaohs.
One of the world's oldest civilizations, known for pyramids, hieroglyphs, and pharaohs

Population & material context: First cities (Uruk ~40–80k), writing (c. 3200), kingship, temple economies (taxation/redistribution), full-time priesthoods, law codes (Hammurabi c. 1750), bronze. World ~14 → 50 M.

Concept of God: Developed polytheistic pantheons + divine council (Anu/Enlil/Enki; Ptah, Ra). El spreads west with the Amorites (c. 2300–1800). Substitute-king ritual & human sacrifice attested.

Mediator: The divine / sacral king (pharaoh as god; Mesopotamian king as the god's steward).

Cosmos & afterlife: Three-tier cosmos; ziggurat = cosmic mountain. Mesopotamian "House of Dust" (grim, neutral, like Sheol); Egypt the early exception — moral judgment of the dead (weighing of the heart).
Ancient creator goddess who wove the world into being on her loom; associated with primordial waters and royal protection.
Sumerian shepherd deity and consort of Inanna; his death and annual lamentation became a major Mesopotamian ritual tradition.
Heliopolitan creator who emerges from the primordial waters; in the Ennead his semen or spittle initiates the first divine generation.
Reconstructed PIE deity of covenant and cosmic order (mitrás); reflected in Vedic Mitra, Mitanni treaty Mitra, and Iranian Mithra. Solar aspects are debated for the proto-form.
First empire in history, established by Sargon of Akkad.
First empire in history, established by Sargon of Akkad

items.n: Migration of Semitic peoples into Egypt
items.d:
Migration of Semitic peoples into Egypt

Significance: Worship of Baal/Seth; early "usurper king" tropes

Notes: West Asian (Semitic, not PIE) origins. The "usurper king" narrative would later be paralleled in the Gaumata story, establishing a pattern of demonizing political rivals as religious imposters.
Supreme ancestral sky deity of the Shang; later Heaven (Tian). Some scholars compare Shangdi to Abrahamic creator concepts, but genetic link is unproven.
Mesopotamian sun and justice god.
Hittite/Hurrian storm god; king of the gods; slayer of the serpent Illuyanka. Comparable to PIE Perkʷunos and the broader Eurasian storm-god complex.
Hittite serpentine chaos monster defeated by the storm god Tarhunna; part of the PIE dragon-slayer complex.
Chief goddess of the Hittite state cult; solar queen of heaven and earth; wife of the storm god Tarhunna.
Hittite deity who disappears causing all fertility to cease and returns restoring it; a disappearing deity motif.
Hurrian deity who castrates Anu and usurps the sky; later overthrown by Teshub. The Kumarbi cycle influenced Hesiod's Theogony.
Hurrian queen of the gods; wife of Teshub/Tarhunna. Major goddess in Hurrian and Hittite state cults.
Sumerian/Akkadian sky god and nominal father of the gods; progenitor of the divine assembly.
Sumerian/Akkadian moon god; parent of Utu/Shamash and Inanna/Ishtar.
Queen of the Sumerian underworld; sister of Inanna; central to the Descent of Inanna myth.
Primordial salt-water ocean dragon slain by Marduk; her body becomes the world. Part of the Near Eastern chaos-dragon complex.
Semi-divine hero king of Uruk; his epic explores heroism, friendship, and the quest for immortality.
Sumerian goddess of writing, grain, and scribal arts; patron of scribes.
Akkadian storm deity cognate with West Semitic Hadad/Baal; controls rain and storms.
Supreme Egyptian solar deity; creator and king of the gods. Merged with Amun as Amun-Ra during the New Kingdom.
Dying-and-rising god, ruler of the dead, and god of resurrection and fertility; murdered by Set, resurrected by Isis.
Goddess of magic, motherhood, and throne; wife of Osiris, mother of Horus. Her mystery cult spread throughout the Roman Empire.
Falcon-headed sky god and divine king; son of Isis and Osiris; battles Set for the throne of Egypt.
God of chaos, storms, the desert, and foreigners; murderer of Osiris; rival of Horus. Also protects Ra's solar barque from Apophis.
Ibis-headed deity of wisdom, writing, and the moon; divine scribe and mediator between Horus and Set.
Cow-headed goddess of love, music, beauty, and fertility; also a goddess of the dead.
Jackal-headed deity of embalming and guide of the dead; presides over the weighing of the heart.
Creator deity who brought the world into being through thought and word; patron of craftsmen. Equated by Greeks with Hephaestus.
Lion-headed goddess of war and plague; also of healing. Aspect of Hathor in her destructive form.
Cosmic chaos serpent who attacks the solar barque of Ra each night; eternally defeated and eternally threatening.
Sky goddess whose body arches over the earth; mother of Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys.
Egyptian earth god; consort of Nut (sky). Father of Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys.
Personification of cosmic order and truth; central to the weighing-of-the-heart judgment and Pharaoh's legitimacy.
Hurrian goddess of love and war; parallel to Ishtar/Inanna; prominent in Hurrian-Hittite religion.
Cat-headed goddess of home, fertility, and protection; popular household deity.
Crocodile god of the Nile, fertility, and pharaonic power.
Famous for Hammurabi's Code and the Hanging Gardens.
Famous for Hammurabi's Code and the Hanging Gardens

items.d:
Rule of Northern Egypt (Delta); capital at Avaris

Significance: Seth (Egyptian storm god identified with Baal)

Notes: Expelled by Ahmose I; Hidden Prince motif: Hyksos rulers demonized as "foreign tyrants." This motif would recur in the Gaumata story and potentially influence narratives about wandering sages and hidden wisdom.
First Chinese dynasty with written records and bronze technology.
Bronze Age Greek civilization, featured in Homer's epics.
First civilization to use iron weapons and establish diplomatic treaties.
First Chinese dynasty with written records and bronze technology
Bronze Age Greek civilization, featured in Homer's epics
First civilization to use iron weapons and establish diplomatic treaties
Queen Mother of the West; goddess of immortality and paradise in Chinese religion.
Earliest Hindu scriptures (Vedas) composed, foundation of Hindu philosophy and practices
Guru-shishya parampara across Vedanta, bhakti, tantra, and yoga traditions in South Asia and the diaspora.
Vedic deity of the three strides; in Vaishnava theology the primary creator who generates Brahma and supplies the material of the cosmos.
Vedic sky father, linguistically cognate with Zeus and Jupiter.
Major Vedic storm and warrior deity, slayer of Vritra, associated with sovereignty and heroic force.
First mortal and ruler of the dead in Vedic tradition; cognate with Iranian Yima and linked to PIE Yemo.
Mythic first man/lawgiver; preserves the name and role of PIE Manu in Indic tradition.
Vedic dawn goddess; cognate with Greek Eos and Latin Aurora.
Vedic divine horse twins, healers and rescuers, close reflexes of the Indo-European Divine Twins.
Goddess associated with river, speech, knowledge, learning, and the arts.
Divine craftsman and architect of the gods; patron of artisans and builders.
Cosmic person whose sacrifice produces the cosmos and social order in the Purusha Sukta.
Vedic fire deity and the most important ritual figure in the Rigveda; carries sacrificial offerings to the gods.
Vedic deity of the ritual intoxicant and the moon; cognate with Iranian Haoma.
Fearsome Vedic deity of storms, disease, and the wild; precursor to Shiva. Ambivalently destructive and healing.
Vedic serpent/dragon adversary of Indra who hoards the waters and cattle; central to the PIE dragon-slayer myth.
Vedic/Hindu earth mother goddess; name and role reflect the reconstructed PIE earth-mother complex.
Vedic figure who brings hidden fire; often compared to Greek Prometheus as fire-bringer.
Vedic god of wind and breath (prana); father of Hanuman in later tradition; associated with Indra.
Vedic hero associated with the recovery of stolen cattle; cognate of PIE Trito in the First Warrior myth.
Twin sister of Yama in Vedic tradition; their dialogue in primordial time explores incest and the origin of human procreation.
Ugaritic sun goddess; daughter of El in the Baal cycle; regulates day–night and the passage of the dead.
Indo-Aryan divine name in Mitanni-Hurrian treaty pantheon (mi-it-ra); attests pre-Vedic Mitra in a Near Eastern diplomatic context.
Solar disk deity elevated to sole creator by Akhenaten in the Amarna period; later suppressed under Tutankhamun.
Moses leads Israelites out of Egypt, receives Ten Commandments, establishes monotheistic tradition

Population & material context: Late-Bronze collapse (~1177); hundreds of highland villages — four-room houses, no pig bones, terracing; segmentary tribal society; iron spreading. Early Israel tens of thousands; world ~50 M.

Concept of God: El heads the council; Yahweh one of El's sons (Deut 32:8–9), a southern storm-warrior from Seir/Edom/Teman. Household polytheism (Asherah).

Mediator: Charismatic "judges" / war-leaders. No king, no messiah yet.

Cosmos & afterlife: Inherited three-tier cosmos; neutral Sheol.
Hebrew divine title/name cluster; often treated as epithet or hypostasis related to El and Yahweh in critical scholarship.
Patriarchal divine name in Genesis; commonly linked to El traditions before full Yahwistic synthesis.
Sons of God / divine council members in early Israelite and Canaanite-adjacent cosmology; antecedent to later angel and Watcher traditions.
Father of the Irish gods (Tuatha Dé Danann); controls seasons and harvests with his magical club and cauldron of abundance.
Irish goddess of war, fate, and sovereignty; associated with the Tuatha Dé Danann and battle omens.
Pan-Celtic deity of skill and light; Irish Lugh Lámhfhada ('Long-Armed') kills Balor. Identified by Romans with Mercury.
Irish goddess of fire, craft, healing, and poetry; her festival Imbolc marks spring. Absorbed into Christianity as Saint Brigid.
Mother goddess of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish tradition; ancestral mother of the Irish gods.
Fomorian giant with a destructive eye; slain by Lugh at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired.
Vedic deity associated with ṛta, binding law, oaths, and cosmic waters.
Indo-Iranian deity of contract and social bond; cognate with Iranian Mithra. Aditya associated with dawn and friendship; paired with Varuna in early Vedic religion.
Solar deity in Vedic and later Hindu tradition.
Supreme god of Zoroastrianism, associated with wisdom, creation, and cosmic truth/order.
Iranian counterpart of Vedic Yama; son of a solar figure and culture hero/king of a golden age.
Avestan deity/personification of victory; name relates to Vedic Vritrahan, epithet of Indra.
Iranian goddess associated with waters, fertility, purity, and royal legitimacy.
Major Mesopotamian goddess of love, war, sexuality, and the planet Venus; influenced later Near Eastern and Mediterranean goddess complexes.
Major Mesopotamian god associated with air, authority, and kingship.
Mesopotamian god of wisdom, freshwater, magic, and craft.
Destructive spirit opposed to Ahura Mazda in Zoroastrian dualism; the principle of lie/evil (druj).
Iranian ritual plant-deity, cognate with Vedic Soma. Central to Zoroastrian ritual practice.
Yazata of obedience to the divine word; important psychopomp figure who accompanies souls after death.
Personification of sacred fire in Zoroastrian tradition; functionally parallel to Vedic Agni.
Yazata of the star Sirius and rainfall; defeats the demon of drought in a cosmic battle.
Luwian sun god; name cognate with PIE Dyēus; represents the solar/sky deity in Anatolian IE tradition.
Mesopotamian god of the underworld and plague; king of the underworld alongside Ereshkigal.
Patron god of Babylon; supreme deity of the Babylonian pantheon; slays Tiamat to create the world (Enuma Elish).
Babylonian/Assyrian deity of writing and wisdom; son of Marduk; holds the tablet of fates.
Anatolian mother goddess; her mystery cult spread to Greece and Rome. Associated with lions, mountains, and ecstatic rituals.
Consort of Cybele; dying-and-rising vegetation deity; his death and resurrection was commemorated in mystery rituals.
Thracian/Phrygian sky and thunder deity associated with serpents and ecstatic mystery rites; later syncreted with Zeus and Dionysus.
Chief Etruscan deity; sky and thunder god; identified with Greek Zeus/Roman Jupiter.
Chief Etruscan goddess; queen of the gods; identified with Hera/Juno.
Etruscan goddess of wisdom and warfare; identified with Athena/Minerva. The Roman Minerva likely borrowed her name from the Etruscan.
Chief Scythian deity described by Herodotus as queen of the gods; associated with hearth fire.
Sky father of the Scythians according to Herodotus; equated with Zeus. Name means 'father' — possibly cognate with Dyēus ph₂tḗr.
Scythian earth goddess; equated with Gaia by Herodotus. Consort of Papaeus.
Mesopotamian warrior god who slays the demon Asag; patron of agriculture and divine justice. Parallels Indra and other IE dragon-slayers.
Etruscan goddess of love and fertility; identified with Greek Aphrodite and Roman Venus.
Etruscan god of wine and vegetation; identified with Dionysus/Bacchus.
Avestan drought demon defeated by Tishtrya; part of the Iranian cosmic combat for rainfall.
Scythian solar deity equated with Apollo by Herodotus; attestation is thin.
Finnish supreme sky and thunder god; chief deity in Finnish folk religion and epic (Kalevala).
Finnish earth mother goddess; consort of Ukko in folk tradition.
Finnish divine smith of the sky; forges the Sampo in the Kalevala.
Finnish god of the forest and hunting.
Hostile mistress of Pohjola in the Kalevala; antagonist to the heroes.
Tocharian B word for god/deity; sparse mythological attestation from the Tarim Basin IE branch.
Tocharian reflex of the IE Yama figure; attested in Tocharian texts with Indo-Iranian parallels.
Etruscan god of boundaries and cultivated land; identified with Roman Silvanus.
Etruscan sun god depicted in tomb art; identified with Greek Helios/Apollo.
Etruscan Apollo figure; central to Etruscan divination and prophecy.
Etruscan underworld demon/guide with hammer; guards the afterlife journey.
Vedic solar deity of impulsion at sunrise; invoked in the Gāyatrī mantra. Member of the Aditya group with Mitra and Sūrya.
Primary Vedic sun god driving the solar chariot; Aditya paired with Mitra and Savitr in early Vedic religion.
Avestan hero Thraētona ('Son of Third') who defeats the three-headed serpent Aži Dahāka and recovers abducted women; Iranian reflex of Trito.
Avestan three-headed dragon who hoards waters and abducts women; defeated by Thraētona; structurally parallel to Vedic Vṛtra.

The seven Holy Immortals—aspects or emanations of Ahura Mazda, each embodying a virtue and associated element (mind, truth, dominion, devotion, wholeness, immortality, and Mazda himself or Spenta Mainyu in some schemes).
Beneficent Holy Spirit in Zoroastrian theology; creative aspect of Ahura Mazda opposed by Angra Mainyu (destructive spirit).
Amesha Spenta of Good Mind; first Amesha Spenta encountered by Zoroaster in visionary tradition; associated with cattle and righteous thought.
Amesha Spenta of Best Truth/Righteousness (Asha); closely linked to sacred fire and cosmic order (Asha/Arta).
Amesha Spenta of Desirable Dominion; associated with metals and righteous worldly power under Ahura Mazda.
Amesha Spenta of Holy Devotion; personification of pious attitude toward creation and the earth.
Amesha Spenta of Wholeness; paired with Ameretat; associated with water and bodily integrity.
Amesha Spenta of Immortality; paired with Haurvatat; associated with plants and enduring life.
Class of evil spirits in Zoroastrianism; originally Indo-Iranian deities reinterpreted as demons and condemned in the Gathas, opposed to Ahura Mazda and the yazatas.
Longest-ruling dynasty in Chinese history, established Confucianism.
Longest-ruling dynasty in Chinese history, established Confucianism

Population & material context: Monarchy, statehood, Temple economy + scribal class; Assyrian then Babylonian pressure; Hezekiah/Josiah centralization = fiscal and cultic consolidation (622 BCE: Hilkiah "finds" Deuteronomy; rural bamot suppressed — reforms largely reversed after Josiah's death at Megiddo, 609 — killed by Necho II against Huldah's explicit oracle that he would die in peace (2 Kgs 22:20 vs 23:29–30), the first failure of the Deuteronomic retribution scheme and the opening of the theodicy crisis the exile then makes unanswerable). Two kingdoms a few hundred thousand; world ~50–100 M.

Concept of God: National Yahweh absorbs Baal's storm functions → monolatry ("Yahweh-alone," 750–586; Exod 20:3–5). Consort Asherah in popular cult. Divine council still visible in archaic strata (Ps 82).

Mediator: The reigning Davidic king = mashiach (anointed).

Cosmos & afterlife: Temple as microcosm (built c. 957). Still neutral Sheol.

Migration from Central Asia into Asian steppes

Significance: Animism, ancestor worship, sky gods, fire rituals

Notes: Eastern Iranian (PIE branch); ancestral Saka kingship myths: divine horsemen linked to solar cults. These solar-deity associations would later influence Mithraic worship among Indo-Iranian peoples, establishing sun worship that bridges Mithra and later Buddhist iconography.
Rabbinic chains of transmission (mesorah), Hasidic dynasties, and teacher-student lineages across Jewish movements.
Yahweh of Hosts; martial–temple epithet emphasizing divine warrior and heavenly army motifs.
Angel of the Lord in Hebrew narrative; debated as hypostasis, messenger, or pre-incarnate manifestation of Yahweh.
Military powerhouse known for siege warfare and administrative efficiency.

items.d:
Migration to Pontic Steppe (north of Black Sea)

Significance: Horse sacrifices, kurgan burials

Notes: The ritual importance of horses in Scythian culture parallels later accounts of both Gautama Buddha's horse Kanthaka and Mithraic bull sacrifice rituals, suggesting possible common Indo-European ritual origins.
National god of Israel; name attested from Kuntillet Ajrud and Mesha Stele onward; theological profile develops from monarchic to exilic literature.
Chief god of the Urartian kingdom; warrior-kingship deity whose cult centers may have influenced later Armenian royal ideology.
Urartian storm and war god; Hurrian Teshub lineage via Urartian state religion.
Iranian deity of contract and covenant, cognate with Vedic Mitra; later increasingly solarized. Yasht 10 solarizes Mithra as all-seeing covenant-keeper and yazata of light.
Yazata of judgment who weighs souls on the bridge of judgment (Chinvat) after death.
Yazata of the sun and light; attested in Yasht 6; part of the solar and luminous yazata complex with Mithra.
Yazata of wind; in Zoroastrian cosmology occupies the space between the realms of good and evil (Yasht 15).
Yazata goddess of waters; sometimes described as wife or daughter of Ahura Mazda in Pahlavi tradition; overlaps functionally with Anahita.
Wrath demon (druj) opposed to Sraosha; prominent daeva of violence in Avestan tradition.
Birthplace of democracy, philosophy, and Western civilization.
Birthplace of democracy, philosophy, and Western civilization
Philosophical texts exploring concepts of Brahman, Atman, and spiritual liberation

Settlement near Black Sea; contact with Greeks; Migration of the Yautiya tribe

Significance: Fire rituals blend with Greek/Near Eastern cults

Notes: Three Sisters motif: Scythian warrior-women interact with Near Eastern elites; Trial of Blood: Scythian princes prove worth via combat. The "three trials" concept would later appear in both Persian royal narratives and Buddhist spiritual journeys.
Pre-Islamic love/moon deity attested in South Arabian and later Arabian sources.
Chief Olympian god of sky, thunder, kingship, and order; name cognate with Dyēus.
Olympian god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses.
Ruler of the underworld and the dead; also associated with wealth beneath the earth.
Olympian goddess of wisdom, strategy, crafts, and civic protection.
Olympian god of prophecy, music, healing/plague, and archery; later strongly solarized.
Goddess of love, beauty, desire, and fertility; likely influenced by Near Eastern goddess traditions.
Olympian god of war and violent battle.
Olympian divine smith and craftsman.
Messenger god, trickster, guide of souls, patron of travelers and boundaries.
Greek dawn goddess, cognate with Vedic Ushas and Latin Aurora.
Greek heroic twin horsemen, protectors and rescuers; major reflex of the Indo-European Divine Twins.
Greek moon goddess; personification of the moon.
Goddess of grain, harvest, and the Eleusinian Mysteries. Name may mean 'earth mother.'
Queen of the underworld and goddess of spring; her abduction by Hades explains seasonal cycles.
God of wine, ecstasy, theater, and vegetation; associated with death-and-rebirth cycles. Possibly of Thracian/Anatolian influence.
Goddess of the hearth fire; parallels Vedic Agni in hearth/sacred fire domain.
Goddess of the hunt, wilderness, and the moon; twin of Apollo. Possibly pre-Greek or Anatolian in origin.
Queen of the Olympians; goddess of marriage and queenship; wife of Zeus.
Primordial serpentine chaos monster defeated by Zeus; structurally parallel to Hittite Illuyanka, Mesopotamian Tiamat, and Vedic Vritra.
Three fate goddesses (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos) who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.
Titan who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity; trickster and culture hero. Parallels noted with Vedic Mātariśvan.
Greek primordial earth mother; mother of the Titans and personification of the earth.
Titan who castrates and overthrows Uranus; father of Zeus. Succession myth parallels the Hurrian Kumarbi cycle.
Greatest Greek hero; attained divine status. Identified with Phoenician Melqart in the Mediterranean world.
Titaness, mother of Zeus and the Olympians; helped conceal Zeus from Cronus. Central to the Greek succession myth influenced by Near Eastern models.
Greek goddess of victory; often depicted as companion of Athena and Zeus.
Roman civilization and empire

Settle in Ciscaucasian Steppe (Kuban river valley)

Significance: Mixed with local cultures, syncretic practices

Notes: Yautiya tribe, akin to the Yaudheyas, migrated due to pressures from the Medes, moving into Iran and later into the Punjab. This migration established cultural links between Iran and northern India that would later facilitate religious exchange. The name similarities between Yautiya/Yaudheya and Gautama are notable, though linguistically complex.

Saka migrate into Central Asia, expel Scythians west

Notes: Rise of the Median Empire; Medes consolidated power in Western Iran. These migrations established Saka presence in regions that would later become centers of both Zoroastrian and Buddhist activity.
Greek sun deity who drives the solar chariot; distinguished from Apollo's later solar identification. Name cognate with PIE seh₂ul.
Greek-Levantine dying-and-rising vegetation god; mourned by Aphrodite; widely compared to Mesopotamian Dumuzi/Tammuz and Near Eastern seasonal rebirth cults.
Three-bodied giant whose cattle Heracles steals; thematic echo of the Trito cattle-raid myth in Graeco-Roman reflexes.
God of boundaries and landmark stones; his stone in the Capitoline temple could not be displaced for Jupiter.
Founded by Zoroaster, introduces concepts of good vs evil, heaven and hell

Zoroaster (Zarathushtra) preaches

Significance: Early Zoroastrian concepts: dualistic cosmology, ethical conduct, future savior figure

Key figures: Zoroaster

Notes: Pre-Achaemenid; early forms of messianic expectations develop. Zoroaster's teachings about Saoshyant (future savior) established messianic concepts that would potentially influence later Mithraic and Buddhist salvific figures, including Maitreya. His emphasis on ethical conduct parallels Buddha's moral teachings.

Pre-Empire Persian tribal influence grows

Key figures: Cambyses I (grandfather of Cambyses II)

Notes: King of Persis. The consolidation of power under early Achaemenids created the political conditions for later religious developments across a vast territory.

Birth of Cyrus the Great

Key figures: Cyrus II

Notes: Future founder of the Achaemenid Empire. Cyrus would later be mythologized as both a liberator and divinely-favored ruler, establishing a template for benevolent kingship that influenced both political and religious narratives about ideal leadership.
Armenian god of contracts, sunlight, and kingship; Armenian reflex of Iranian Mithra with distinct temple cult.
Armenian goddess of war and wisdom; associated with Amazonian martial iconography in Armenian tradition.
Armenian god of writing, oracles, and astral order; identified with Apollo/Hermes in Hellenistic interpretatio.
Armenian new-year and agricultural festival deity associated with spring renewal and sowing.
Armenian god of hospitality and guest-right; protector of travelers and hosts.
Armenian chthonic earth and fertility goddess; reflex of Zoroastrian Spenta Armaiti in Armenian cult.
Armenian sea/lake goddess of thunder and rain; associated with lightning over waters.
Armenian sky/lord of heaven figure; name and function suggest Semitic Baal/Bel-type influence.
Armenian spring and resurrection festival figure linked to renewal of nature and ritual rebirth.
Obscure Armenian divine name preserved in fragmentary pre-Christian references.
Obscure Armenian divine or cult title; possibly related to earth or fertility vocabulary.
Armenian dog-spirit that licks fallen heroes to restore them to life in epic folklore. Indigenous healing-spirit motif in epic tradition.
Armenian giant/demon figure of epic and folklore; often antagonist in heroic narratives. Chaos giant of Armenian oral epic; Zoroastrian daeva language may color later accounts.
Armenian folk giant or ogre figure; preserves older Caucasian supernatural vocabulary. Folk antagonist type; substrate figure predating formal temple pantheon.
Armenian folk demon associated with childbirth and the margins of domestic space. Female demon of folklore; attestation primarily post-pagan but likely older substrate.
Armenian water serpent/demon of rivers and lakes; related to vishap dragon lore. Aquatic dragon-serpent of Armenian folklore.
Armenian dragon being of storm, water, and fertility; linked to vishapakar standing stones. Central dragon figure; may preserve pre-IE Caucasian religious strata.
Guardian spirit of district, district-boundary, or settlement in Armenian tradition. Tutelary district spirit; Persian shah + Armenian pet ('guardian').
Obscure Armenian folk spirit or demon attested in later folklore collections. Fragmentary folklore attestation.

Population & material context: Jerusalem & Temple destroyed; Judean elite deported; others flee to Egypt. Loss of king + land + Temple forces religion onto text / Torah.

Concept of God: Ontological monotheism — "there is no other" (Deutero-Isaiah). God deterritorialized & mobile (Ezekiel's chariot-throne).

Mediator: A future ideal Davidide hoped for; strikingly, the foreign king Cyrus is called mashiach (Isa 45:1).

Cosmos & afterlife: Cosmos abstracted & moralized; Genesis 1 (Priestly) ordered creation. Sheol persists, but pressure for justice begins.

Birth of Cassandane Shahbanu

Key figures: Cassandane

Notes: Principal wife of Cyrus II, mother of Cambyses II and Atossa. Her death triggered empire-wide mourning, demonstrating how royal women could inspire devotion comparable to religious figures.
Siddhartha Gautama born, later becomes Buddha and establishes Buddhist teachings

[lineage-seed:buddhism:shakyamuni] Root of the Buddhist tradition. Teacher whose disciples preserved the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma, and whose awakening became the reference point for all later schools.

Birth of Bardiya (Smerdis)

Key figures: Bardiya (Smerdis)

Notes: Son of Cyrus the Great, younger brother of Cambyses II. His contested identity and fate would become central to religious and political narratives about legitimacy, potentially influencing stories about hidden or misunderstood spiritual leaders like Gautama Buddha.

Cyrus becomes King of Anshan

Key figures: Cyrus II

Notes: Inherits throne of Anshan, a vassal kingdom under Median rule. Cyrus's rise from vassal to emperor parallels spiritual narratives about transformation from ordinary being to enlightened one.
One of the largest empires in history, stretching from Egypt to India.
One of the largest empires in history, stretching from Egypt to India

items.n: Cyrus overthrows Astyages; birth of Atossa
items.d:
Cyrus overthrows Astyages; birth of Atossa

Significance: Establishment of the Achaemenid Empire

Key figures: Cyrus II, Astyages, Atossa

Notes: Cyrus revolts against Median overlord; Atossa (daughter of Cyrus, later wife of Cambyses II and Darius I). The overthrow of established order parallels religious narratives about spiritual revolution against entrenched dogma, as seen in both Mithraic mysteries and Buddha's challenge to Brahmanical orthodoxy.

items.n: Cyrus expands east; builds fortresses against Saka; defeats Saka Haumavarga
items.d:
Cyrus expands east; builds fortresses against Saka; defeats Saka Haumavarga

Significance: Zoroastrianism (Mazdaism) introduced; local traditions persist

Key figures: Cyrus II

Notes: Achaemenid control established over eastern Iranian and northwestern Indian regions. This expansion brought Persian religious concepts into direct contact with Indic traditions, creating the syncretic environment where both Mithraic mysteries and early Buddhism would develop. The Saka Haumavarga ("haoma-drinking Saka") practiced rituals involving sacred beverages that parallel both Mithraic ritual feasts and early Buddhist discussions of soma.

Cyrus captures Sardis

Key figures: Cyrus II, Croesus

Notes: Defeat of Croesus brings Asia Minor under Persian control. The Lydian-Persian cultural contact introduced monetary economy concepts that would later influence both Mithraic cult finances and Buddhist monastic organization.

Connection between Utians and Yautiya

Notes: Behistun Inscription mentions "Vautiya" region, connected to Herodotus's "Utians." These tribal connections between central Iranian plateau and northern India established pathways for religious ideas to travel between regions that would later develop Mithraism and Buddhism.

Artunis commands Persian military

Key figures: Artunis

Notes: Military leader under Cyrus II; represented Persian women's roles in warfare. Female leadership in Persian society contrasts with later religious traditions but may have influenced early Buddhist inclusion of women as disciples.

Population & material context: Return + Second Temple (c. 516); Yehud a small temple-state; Torah codified (Ezra–Nehemiah); priesthood = governing class under empire; Aramaic lingua franca; diaspora permanent. Popular religion still polytheistic (Elephantine).

Concept of God: Monotheism consolidated; metaphysical expansion — named angels, Satan splitting off, cosmic dualism (Zoroastrian-tinged).

Mediator: Future Davidic hope continues.

Cosmos & afterlife: Transcendent heaven displaces the localized mountain; judgment emerges.

items.n: Cyrus conquers Babylon; Pantea Arteshbod at Battle of Opis
items.d:
Cyrus conquers Babylon; Pantea Arteshbod at Battle of Opis

Key figures: Cyrus II, Nabonidus, Pantea Arteshbod

Notes: Incorporation of Mesopotamia; Cyrus allows Jews to return to Jerusalem; Pantea was key strategist in conquest. Cyrus's religious tolerance established a precedent for pluralism that would characterize regions where Mithraic and Buddhist ideas later flourished alongside local traditions.

New Year Festival Ritual

Key figures: Cambyses II, Cyrus II

Notes: Cambyses received royal sceptre in Esagila (temple to Marduk). This ritual legitimization of rule through religious ceremony would be paralleled in later Buddhist royal patronage and Mithraic initiation ceremonies.

items.n: Cambyses appointed Governor of Northern Babylonia
items.d:
Cambyses appointed Governor of Northern Babylonia

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: Held title "King of Babylon, King of the Lands." The delegation of power prefigures administrative systems that would later support religious institutions across the empire.

Cambyses dismissed from governorship

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: Continued to reside in Babylonian cities. This earliest recorded instance of Cambyses's unstable governance foreshadows the later instability that would allow Gaumata's rise.

items.n: Expedition against Massagetae; Death of Cyrus
items.d:
Expedition against Massagetae; Death of Cyrus

Key figures: Cyrus II, Cambyses II

Notes: Cambyses participated but was sent back to Persia before Cyrus' fatal encounter. Cyrus's death fighting eastern Iranian tribes established a narrative about the dangers of the frontier that would later color accounts of eastern religious developments. The Massagetae, related to Saka tribes, maintained religious practices connecting Iranian and Central Asian traditions.

Succession and Co-rulership

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: Appointed as co-ruler by Cyrus; carried father's body to Pasargadae for burial. The ritualized treatment of royal remains parallels later religious concepts about the sacred nature of enlightened bodies in Buddhism.

Controversial marriage of Atossa

Significance: Marriage reinforced dynastic purity but drew Greek condemnation

Key figures: Atossa, Cambyses II

Notes: Persian royal tradition viewed such unions as preserving "divine bloodline." This concept of maintaining pure lineage would later find parallels in both Mithraic initiation lines and Buddhist teacher-disciple lineages claiming direct connection to founders.

items.n: Bardiya appointed governor of eastern provinces
items.d:
Bardiya appointed governor of eastern provinces

Key figures: Bardiya

Notes: Included governance of Bactria. This placement of Bardiya (later known as Gaumata) in the eastern regions directly connects him to areas that would become centers of both Mithraic and Buddhist development. His time in Bactria and proximity to Gandhara would have exposed him to emerging religious ideas later associated with both traditions.
Buddha achieves enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, begins teaching the Four Noble Truths

Political preparations for Egyptian conquest

Key figures: Cambyses II, Amasis II, Polycrates

Notes: Death of Amasis II weakened Egypt; Polycrates of Samos allied with Cambyses. These diplomatic maneuvers demonstrate the interconnectedness of Mediterranean and Near Eastern worlds, creating networks through which religious ideas could travel.

Naval and diplomatic preparations

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: Created Persian navy using Phoenician resources; treaty with Arabs to secure water supply. The logistical preparations for conquest established routes that would later facilitate spread of religious ideas, including Mithraic mysteries toward the west.

Conquest of Egypt

Key figures: Cambyses II, Psamtik III

Notes: Defeated Egyptian forces at Pelusium; captured Memphis. This conquest brought Egyptian solar theology into contact with Persian religious ideas, potentially influencing the development of solar aspects in both Mithraism and later Buddhist iconography.

Egyptian Rule

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: Adopted Egyptian royal titles; crowned at Sais temple; claimed descent from Egyptian royalty. This religious syncretism at the highest levels set precedents for later fusion of Persian, Greek, and Indian religious concepts.

Treatment of Apis Bull

Significance: Contrary to later hostile accounts, participated in preservation ceremony

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: The reverential treatment of the Apis bull contradicts later Greek propaganda and demonstrates Persian respect for local animal cults. This parallels later veneration of animals in both Mithraic (bull) and Buddhist (elephant, horse) traditions.

Cambyses orders execution of Smerdis (disputed)

Key figures: Cambyses II, Smerdis

Notes: According to Darius's Behistun Inscription; highly disputed claim. This contested narrative about Bardiya/Smerdis's death parallels narratives of spiritual teachers who appear to die yet continue to influence followers. Some scholars speculate that if Bardiya survived and fled east, he could have encountered or even influenced emerging religious communities in regions that would later develop Buddhism.

Cambyses departs from Egypt

Key figures: Cambyses II, Aryandes

Notes: Left to deal with rebellion; appointed Aryandes as governor of Egypt. The rebellion that drew Cambyses back was ostensibly led by Gaumata claiming to be Bardiya, establishing the pattern of contested identity that recurs in religious narratives about authentic vs. false teachers.

Death of Cambyses II

Key figures: Cambyses II

Notes: Died under mysterious circumstances in Syria; infected leg wound from sword when mounting horse. The mysterious death created a power vacuum that allowed Gaumata/Bardiya to claim the throne. The motif of a ruler dying from a wound parallels later religious narratives about suffering and transformation.

Gaumata seizes power

Key figures: Gaumata/Bardiya

Notes: Claims to be Bardiya and seizes power; supported by anti-Cambyses factions. Gaumata introduced religious reforms, including tax relief and changes to temple administration that some scholars compare to both Mithraic social egalitarianism and Buddha's rejection of excessive ritual costs. His brief rule represents a syncretic moment when Persian religious practice might have been steered toward more universalist tendencies similar to those that would characterize both Mithraism and Buddhism.

Gaumata's coup & female backlash

Key figures: Sisygambis

Notes: noblewomen

Irdabama's economic empire

Key figures: Irdabama

Notes: Wealthiest businesswoman; oversaw wine/grain trade across 5 regions. Her economic power demonstrates the potential for non-royal individuals to influence imperial affairs, similar to how merchants would later support Buddhist monasteries.

Revolts against Gaumata

Key figures: Various faction leaders

Notes: Multiple regions resist Gaumata/Bardiya. The fragmentation of authority during this period may have allowed heterodox religious ideas to develop in provincial areas, particularly in eastern regions that would later become centers of Buddhism.

Revolt of Vahyazdâta

Key figures: Vahyazdâta, Darius I, Artavardiya

Notes: Claimed to be Bardiya; many Persians supported him. The multiple claimants to Bardiya's identity suggest the powerful appeal of the reformist religious policies Gaumata/Bardiya had instituted, prefiguring the popular appeal of both Mithraic and Buddhist teachings.

Vahyazdâta's challenge to Darius

Key figures: Vahyazdâta, Vivana

Notes: Attempted to capture Kabul Valley; defeated by satrap of Harahvatis. The focus on controlling regions that would later become Buddhist heartlands suggests their strategic importance to the empire.

Battle at Rakhâ

Key figures: Vahyazdâta, Artavardiya

Notes: Artavardiya suppressed Vahyazdâta's rebellion. The systematic suppression of Bardiya-claimants established a pattern of orthodoxy triumphing over reform that would be mirrored in later religious conflicts.

Assassination of Gaumata

Key figures: Darius I, six Persian nobles

Notes: Palace coup at Sikayauvati. The violent overthrow of Gaumata mirrors the later Buddhist narrative of Mara's assault on the Buddha, with Darius potentially serving as a template for forces opposing spiritual revolution. Some scholars speculate that if Gaumata survived (as later rumors suggested), his flight eastward could connect to emergence of wandering teachers in northwestern India.

Rebellions against Darius

Key figures: Various leaders

Notes: Elam, Media, and Persia see uprisings. The widespread resistance to Darius suggests Gaumata/Bardiya's reforms had significant popular support, similar to how both Mithraic and Buddhist teachings would later appeal to various social classes seeking alternatives to established orders.

items.n: Darius consolidates Achaemenid rule; regions listed in Behistun Inscription
items.d:
Darius consolidates Achaemenid rule; regions listed in Behistun Inscription

Significance: Zoroastrianism and Iranian cults (e.g., Mithra) spread; syncretism with local beliefs

Key figures: Darius I

Notes: Taxila (Takṣaśila) becomes major center for learning and religious exchange. If Gaumata/Bardiya did escape east after being deposed, this period coincides with the traditional dating of Buddha's lifetime, raising speculative connections between Persian religious reformers and emerging Buddhist teachings. Taxila's importance as a learning center could have facilitated transmission of ideas between Persian and Indian traditions.

Vahyazdata rises in Persia

Key figures: Vahyazdata

Notes: Persian rebel claiming to be Bardiya; rose in Tārvā (Yautiya district). The persistent emergence of Bardiya-claimants suggests a messianic quality attributed to him, potentially influencing later concepts of returning savior figures in both Mithraic (Mithra's return) and Buddhist (Maitreya) traditions.

Battle of Rakhâ

Key figures: Vahyazdata, Artavardiya

Notes: Vahyazdata's forces defeated by Darius' general. The repeated military suppression of reform movements established a pattern of orthodoxy using force against religious innovation.

Battle at Parga

Key figures: Vahyazdâta, Artavardiya

Notes: Vahyazdâta fled after defeat but gathered another army. The persistence of resistance despite defeats parallels narratives about religious communities surviving persecution.

Battle of Parga

Key figures: Vahyazdata, Artavardiya

Notes: Vahyazdata defeated and captured. His capture represents the temporary triumph of imperial orthodoxy over reform movements.

Second battle in Arachosia

Key figures: Vahyazdâta's commander, Vivâna

Notes: Rebels regrouped but defeated at Gandutava. The focus on controlling Arachosia (near Gandhara) highlights the region's importance as a frontier zone where heterodox ideas could flourish.

Execution of Vahyazdâta

Key figures: Vahyazdâta

Notes: Crucified with chief supporters in Uvâdaicaya. The public execution through crucifixion established a martyrdom narrative that parallels later religious stories about persecution of truth-bringers. Some scholars note similarities between these executions and later accounts of religious persecution in both western and eastern traditions.

Rebel forces defeated

Key figures: Vivâna

Notes: Forces sent by Vahyazdata defeated at Kapishkanish (Kandahar). This region would later become a crucial center for Buddhist development, suggesting continuity between political resistance to imperial orthodoxy and religious innovation.

Final battle at Gandutava

Key figures: Vivâna

Notes: Remaining rebels loyal to Vahyazdata crushed. Despite military defeat, the ideals associated with Gaumata/Bardiya may have survived among displaced populations moving eastward.

Last supporters hunted down

Notes: Final elimination of Vahyazdâta's supporters. The thorough persecution may have forced surviving adherents to flee further east, potentially carrying syncretic religious ideas into regions where Buddhism would later develop.

Darius consolidates power

Key figures: Darius I

Notes: Executes further rivals; establishes legitimacy. Darius's narrative about defeating the "false Bardiya" created a template for religious orthodoxy defining itself against "illegitimate" teachers that would reappear in later religious polemics.

items.n: Darius's campaigns against Saka; captures King Skunxa
items.d:
Darius's campaigns against Saka; captures King Skunxa

Key figures: Darius I, Skunxa

Notes: Territories incorporated into Achaemenid Empire as part of Chorasmia. The eastern campaigns brought Persian administrative systems into regions where both Mithraic and Buddhist ideas would flourish, potentially creating conditions for syncretism between Persian royal ideology and indigenous spiritual practices.

Atossa's political influence peaks

Key figures: Atossa, Darius I

Notes: Persuaded Darius to name Xerxes as heir over older half-brothers. Her influence demonstrates how Cyrus's bloodline maintained sacred status even after the purging of Bardiya/Gaumata, paralleling how religious lineages maintain authority through selective interpretation of founder's legacies.
Second Temple built in Jerusalem, centralization of Jewish worship and law

items.n: Darius's Scythian Expedition across the Danube
items.d:
Darius's Scythian Expedition across the Danube

Key figures: Darius I

Notes: Outcome debated; some Achaemenid authority may have been established. The westward campaigns demonstrated Persian interest in controlling Scythian/Saka populations in all directions, potentially influencing how Mithraic ideas would later spread both east and west from Persian heartlands.
Founded by Confucius, emphasizes moral values, social harmony, and filial piety

Achaemenid administration; Persian satraps govern

Significance: Zoroastrian and Mithraic cults influence local practices; Buddhist and Jain ideas emerge

Notes: Early Buddhist concepts show possible Mazdean influence. This century of Persian administrative control coincides with the traditional period of early Buddhist development, suggesting opportunities for Persian religious concepts to influence emerging Buddhist teachings. Concepts potentially shared between traditions include cosmic dualism, ethical focus, and messianic expectations. The name similarities between Gaumata and Gautama, while linguistically distinct, have prompted speculation about narrative parallels between the Persian reformer and the Buddha.

Settlement of Rohitas and Yautiya

Key figures: Rohitas, Yautiya

Notes: Settled in East Punjab, Rajasthan, later in Rohilkhand, Uttar Pradesh. These tribal settlements may have carried memories of the Gaumata affair and Persian religious concepts into regions that would become centers of Buddhist activity.

Rise of incest accusations

Notes: Greek historians allege royal intermarriage; modern scholars argue claims exaggerated. The Greek polemics against Persian customs parallels how orthodox traditions often demonize heterodox religious movements, a pattern seen in both Darius's treatment of Gaumata and later religious polemics against Mithraism and early Buddhism.

items.d:
Saka tribes listed as Achaemenid subjects

Notes: Supplying troops and tribute; some act as allies, others maintain autonomy. The incorporation of Saka troops into Persian armies facilitated cultural exchange, potentially spreading both Mithraic and emerging Buddhist ideas along military routes. The Saka's semi-autonomous status allowed them to maintain distinct religious practices that could bridge Persian and Indian traditions.

Divine physician and healer of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
Horse goddess of fertility, travel, and protection; widely venerated in Gaul and the Roman army.
Enigmatic Gaulish god connected with forests, trees, and sacrifice in Lucan's account.

Irish sovereignty and war goddess connected with Ulster; one aspect of the Morrígan complex.
Sea god and psychopomp associated with the Otherworld, weather, and magical mist.

Healing, hunting, and sea god worshipped at Lydney Park in Roman Britain.
Silver-handed first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
Champion god of eloquence, poetry, and strength; inventor of the Ogham script in Irish tradition.
Welsh horse-associated goddess of sovereignty and the Otherworld; figure of the Mabinogi.
Legendary warrior woman and martial teacher of Cú Chulainn on the Isle of Skye.
Hammer-bearing Gaulish god associated with agriculture, forests, and wine or beer.
Thunder god symbolized by the wheel and lightning across Gaul and Britain.

Protective tribal deity worshipped across Gaul and Britain.
Giant king and Otherworld figure associated with protection, sacrifice, and the severed head motif.

Star- and moon-associated Welsh goddess connected to fate, virginity, and rebirth.
Lord of the dead and ruler of Tech Duinn, the house of the departed.
Goddess of beauty and the Otherworld; associated with the sea and the wave of Glandore.
River goddess of the Boyne; her trespass on the Otherworld well scatters wisdom.
Goddess of summer, fertility, wealth, and sovereignty in Munster tradition.
Earth and harvest goddess commemorated in the Lughnasadh festival.

Sea and Otherworld goddess tied to love and desire; wife of Manannán in some tales.
Beautiful but tyrannical king associated with the Fomorians and brief Tuatha Dé Danann rule.
Fairy queen and supernatural guardian spirit of Thomond.
Otherworld lord associated with magic, music, and immortality; rival of Aengus for Étaín.
Forest and river goddess linked to the Black Forest and Danubian regions.
Healing goddess associated with springs and serpents in Gaul and the Rhineland.
River goddess of the Seine; worshipped at the Burgundian source sanctuary.
Bright goddess of fire, craftsmanship, and light in Gaulish tradition.
Sea deity and father of Manannán mac Lir in Irish genealogies.
Divine figure associated with fire and the underworld in Irish genealogical lore.
Divine bronze worker and craftsman of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
Blind druidic magician associated with prophecy, flying, and storms.
Supernatural race of divine beings in Irish mythology who succeed the Fomorians.
Chaotic primordial beings often opposing the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish myth.
Fairy folk or Otherworld beings dwelling in mounds (síd) in Irish and Scottish lore.
Welsh divine family roughly parallel to the Tuatha Dé Danann in medieval Welsh literature.
Hindu creator god of the Trimurti; in Puranic theology often a secondary fashioner born from Vishnu (or Shiva) who shapes the universe from primordial materials rather than creating ex nihilo.
Goddess of wealth, beauty, fortune, prosperity, and auspiciousness.
Divine war leader and commander, especially important in South Indian traditions as Murugan.
Divine sage and messenger who moves between worlds, often catalyzing events through speech and music.

Complex of Hindu great goddess manifestations: Parvati (benign), Durga (warrior demon-slayer), Kali (fierce destroyer). Aspects of Devi/Shakti.
Elephant-headed deity, remover of obstacles, patron of scribes and learners; son of Shiva and Parvati.
Class of nature spirits associated with wealth and fertility; Kubera is their king and the Hindu god of wealth.
Major avatar of Vishnu; central deity of the Bhakti tradition.
Seventh avatar of Vishnu; hero of the Ramayana; ideal king and embodiment of dharma.
Fierce goddess of time and destruction; form of Devi/Shakti; distinct cult from benign Parvati.
Supreme divine feminine power (Shakti) underlying Durga, Kali, Parvati, and Lakshmi manifestations.
Middle Persian and Parthian solarized form of Mithra; attested in inscriptions and Sogdian/Parthian iconography as sun god and covenant-keeper.
Palmyrene sun god and oath-keeper (Maran Mithra, 'Our Lord Mithra'); syncretic Near Eastern solar cult with Iranian Mithra and Roman Sol themes.
Roman Hercules (Greek Heracles) with distinct Roman cult at the Ara Maxima; god of strength and boundary-crossing hero.
Plebeian triad of Ceres, Liber, and Libera established on the Aventine Hill c. 493 BC.
Female counterpart of Liber in the Aventine Triad; later assimilated to Proserpina/Persephone.

Artaynte affair

Key figures: Artaynte, Xerxes I

Notes: Alleged affair with Xerxes led Masistes to rebel; Xerxes executed Masistes and sons. The court intrigues demonstrate continuing tensions within the Achaemenid dynasty that may have influenced religious narratives about moral corruption and renewal.
Founded by Laozi, emphasizes living in harmony with the Tao (the Way)

items.n: Saka and Scythian migrations intensify; Achaemenid control wanes
items.d:
Saka and Scythian migrations intensify; Achaemenid control wanes

Significance: Religious syncretism: Greek, Iranian, and Indian elements merge

Notes: Zoroastrian sanctuaries found in Taxila; Mithra worship persists among Saka. This period of religious mixing coincides with the development of Mahayana Buddhism, which incorporates more explicit savior concepts similar to those in Mithraic tradition. The continued presence of Mithra worship among Saka tribes provides a potential link between Persian religious concepts and developing Buddhist ideas about cosmic buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Chief god of pre-Islamic Mecca; oracle deity whose cult was centered at the Kaaba before Islamic reform.
Eponymous forefather of Armenians; defeats Bel/Nimrod in national foundation epic (Khorenatsi).
Legendary Armenian king whose beauty draws Shamiram; central figure in Armenian romantic epic.
Armenian epic queen; assimilated Semiramis legend into Armenian national narrative.
Tragic royal figure in Armenian epic tradition; son of Artashes, bound in mountain legend.
Legendary ugly hero of Armenian folklore; embodies indigenous warrior substrate motifs.
Hero of Armenian epic cycles; brother of Baghdasar in Sasun-related traditions.
Epic hero paired with Sanasar in Armenian oral tradition.
Central hero of the Armenian Daredevils of Sassoun epic cycle; Christian-era national epic figure.
Hero of Sassoun epic; associated with immortality and the closed door (chthonic/warrior themes).
Younger Mher of the Sassoun cycle; tragic hero who opens the forbidden door.
Roman Apollo, imported from Greek religion; god of poetry, music, oracles, and healing; twin of Diana; one of the Dii Consentes.
Craftsman god in Plato's Timaeus who orders pre-existing matter into the cosmos; distinct from the Abrahamic ex nihilo creator and from later Gnostic demiurge traditions.

Sisygambis' diplomatic role

Key figures: Sisygambis

Notes: Mother of Darius III; after defeat by Alexander, negotiated family's safety. Her role demonstrates the continuing importance of royal women in Persian politics, a pattern that would influence how female patronage operated in later religious traditions.

Population & material context: Alexander → Greek koine, Diadochi kingdoms, Alexandrian Judaism, Septuagint; Maccabean revolt (167); apocalyptic sectarianism (Qumran). World ~150–200 M.

Concept of God: Hypostatic expansion — Wisdom / Sophia as cosmic agent; "two powers in heaven"; Greek metaphysics reinforces transcendence.

Mediator: Priestly messiah (Qumran's two messiahs) and the apocalyptic "Son of Man" (Daniel 7, c. 165).

Cosmos & afterlife: Heavenly Temple; cosmic dualism. Bodily resurrection + last judgment explicit (Daniel 12, c. 165).

Saka oppose Alexander the Great

Notes: Sometimes allying with Bactrians and Sogdians against him. The resistance to Hellenization demonstrates continuing Indo-Iranian cultural solidarity that would influence how both Mithraic and Buddhist traditions incorporated or resisted Greek elements.

items.n: Alexander conquers region; Greek satraps established

Notes: Gandhara art blends Greek, Iranian, and Buddhist motifs. The iconographic development of Buddha images during this period shows striking parallels to Mithraic imagery, including solar halos, royal postures, and cosmic symbolism. Some scholars suggest the story of Gaumata's brief rule and violent overthrow may have influenced Buddhist narratives about opposition to enlightened teaching.

Indo-Greek and Saka kingdoms rise

Significance: Maitreya concept develops, possibly influenced by Mithraic messianic ideas

Notes: The concept of Maitreya, the future Buddha, emerges. Maitreya's development as a messianic figure parallels both Zoroastrian Saoshyant and Mithraic savior concepts, suggesting potential influence from Persian religious traditions transmitted through Saka intermediaries. The name "Maitreya" itself relates linguistically to "Mithra," suggesting possible conceptual borrowing between traditions.

Significance: Development of Mahayana Buddhism; Maitreya becomes important

Key figures: Kushan kings

Notes: Royal Messiahs: Kushan kings claim divine lineage. Kushan royal ideology blended Iranian concepts of divine kingship with Buddhist patronage, creating syncretism at the highest political levels. Some kings used titles like "Son of Heaven" that echo both Persian and Chinese imperial terminology while supporting Buddhist institutions.

Population & material context: Small hybrid kingdom on border of Hasmonean Judea; Nomos (~62 BCE) equates Mithra = Apollo-Helios-Hermes; lion horoscope at Nemrud dated astronomically to ~7 July 62 BCE — royal astral cult. Missing middle between Achaemenid Mithra and Roman Mithras. See michael-mithra-christ Part IV, §25b.

Concept of God: Elite Iranian–Greek divine fusion in official ideology; solar–Hermetic Mithra; astral legitimation of kingship.

Mediator: Royal horoscope as epoch marker; not Jewish messiah — but ambient astral-court environment parallel to Daniel/Enoch.

Cosmos & afterlife: Planets and host of heaven as cosmic powers — parallel structural environment for Jewish apocalyptic celestial court.

Population & material context: Pax Romana — roads, koine, urban diaspora networks become the vector for Christian spread. Temple destroyed 70 CE. Empire ~45–60 M (~25% of humanity); Christians a tiny sect → perhaps ~10% of the empire by 300. World ~200 M.

Concept of God: Logos Christology; pre-existent Christ → the Trinity (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Chalcedon 451). Constantine (312) → state religion under Theodosius (380).

Mediator: Christ — the fusion of king, Son of Man, Wisdom/Logos, and pre-existent messiah.

Cosmos & afterlife: New Jerusalem / heavenly Temple (Revelation c. 95); developed heaven & hell, resurrection, final judgment.

Population & material context: Antonine & Cyprianic plagues; Western Rome falls (476); Christianization of the Mediterranean. Sacrifice ends → synagogue + Torah-study Judaism. World ~200 M.

Concept of God: Judaism: Torah-centered, imageless, transcendent God met through study & law; Shekhinah (indwelling presence) develops; "two powers" policed as heresy. Christianity: Trinitarian God fixed dogmatically.

Mediator: Judaism: the Torah itself + a future messiah. Christianity: the incarnate Logos + the Church.

Cosmos & afterlife: Augustine — original sin, predestination, the two cities; resurrection + heaven/hell (purgatory formalized later).

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:phagmo-drupa] Pakmodrupa was a disciple of Gampopa and is one of the earliest patriarchs of the Kagyu tradition. His monastery, Densatil , which he founded in 1158, was the training ground for most of the founders of the Kagyu sub-traditions, such as Taklungtangpa and Jikten Gonpo , who went on to establish the Taklung and Drigung Kagyu, respectively. He integrated teachings that he received from Kadam, Sakya and, in vision, Zhije instructors into those he received from Gampopa. A widely learned but humble monk, he gave a clear priority to meditation over textual scholarship and philosophical reflection. His collected works have only recently been published in full. [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gompa-tsultrim-nyingpo] Gompo Tsultrim Nyingpo, popularly known as Gomtsul, served as abbot of Daklha Gampo , the 'headquarters' of the Kagyu school, for nineteenth years following the death of his uncle Gampopa. He played an important historical role in his mediation of warring factions associated with different monastic lineages in the Lhasa area during the twelfth century. He was in charge of restoring the J okang Temple , since it had suffered serious damage during the fighting. He founded a monastery named Tsur Lhalung in Tolung. The most renowned among his disciples was Lama Zhang Yudrakpa . (BDRC P1845)

An expert in Nyingma tantra, his compositions are collected in nine volumes. (BDRC P1314)

He is widely regarded as the one Tibetan who best exemplifies the Indian ideal of the Mahasiddha. (BDRC P910)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chegompa-sherab-dorje] Chegompa Sherab Dorje is a mystifying figure for students of Tibetan Buddhism. He is widely accepted as a Kadampa, and certainly does hold a Kadam lineage. Still, in his best-known work he lays emphasis on simultaneous Mahāmudrā teachings, which were usually not in favor with Kadampas. Some think he had connections with the Tselpa Kagyu, although more certainly he was affiliated with the Tropu Kagyu. He was important for the transmission of the Kadam text known as the Example Teachings ( dpe chos ) and wrote a commentary on it, but he is probably best known for his Precious Heap of Instructions ( man ngag rin chen spungs pa ). Today his works are most greatly treasured by the Geluk. (BDRC P4892)

[rigpa-wiki:Lama Jangchub Rinpoche] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gomchung-sherab-jangchub] Gomchung Sherab Jangchub was a nephew of Gampopa and a younger brother of Gomtsul. He served as the third abbot of Daklha Gampo after the death of Gomtsul. (BDRC P1841)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:dakpo-duldzin] Dakpo Duldzin was the fourth abbot of Daklha Gampo , the earliest Kagyu Monastery. [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lhachug-kharwa-nyida-o] Lhachuk Kharwa was one of the four main disciples of Lama Zhang Yudrakpa . He founded the Lhachuk Monastery in 1193 and became the abbot of Tsel Monastery in 1210. During his abbacy, or soon after his death, the Tselpa Kagyu spread in the westernmost parts of the Tibetan Plateau. (BDRC P4139)

[rigpa-wiki:Chöjé Marpa Sherab Yeshé] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:marpa-sherab-yeshe] Marpa Sherab Yeshe was the founder of the Martsang Kagyu, one of a number of lineages that descended through disciples of Pakmodrupa . [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsangton-dorje-gyeltsen] Tsangton Dorje Gyeltsen, a close disciple of Katokpa Dampa Deshek , was the second abbot of Katok Monastery , from 1192 to his death in 1227. (BDRC P7894)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rokam-nyima-sherab] Rokam Nyima Sherab served and studied with Zhang Yudrakpa before he founded his own monastery at Rokam . He was a significant figure in the early history of the Tselpa Kagyu. He initiated a lineage belonging to the Bar Tsel, the ‘Middle Lineage of the Tselpa Kagyu.’ (BDRC P2470)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drubtob-nyakre-sewo] Drubtob Nyakre Sewo was a disciple of Pakmodrupa and Jikten Gonpo . [lineage-seed:zhije-chod-lineage:zarawa-kelden-yeshe-sengge] Zhije lineage holder in the Tingri tradition of Phadampa Sangye.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:spyan-snga-rin-chen-bzang-po] Chennga Rinchen Zangpo was a disciple of  Jikten Gonpo Rinchen Pel , the founder of  Drigung Til Monastery . He spent much of his life in Rebkong, spreading the Drigung teaching to lay disciples. (BDRC P11MS249)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:zarawa-kalden-yeshe-sengge] Zarawa Kelden Yeshe Sengge was one of the four foremost disciples of Pakmodrupa . [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sanggye-dorje] Sanggye Dorje was the second abbot of Rokam Monastery . (BDRC P4168)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:yabzang-choje-chokyi-monlam] Yabzang Choje Chokyi Monlam was founder of the Yabzang Kagyu lineage, named after Yabzang Monastery , which he founded in 1206. (BDRC P4322)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:pomdrakpa] Pomdrakpa Sonam Dorje was an important early Karma Kagyu lineage holder; he was a student of Sanggye Rechen and a teacher of the Second Karmapa, Karma Pakshi, whom he identified as the reincarnation of the First Karmapa. He took over and renovated Tasho Pomdrak monastery. (BDRC P2438)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rinchen-sherab] Zhikpo Rinchen Sherab was the younger brother of Rokben Sherab O and a disciple of the same teacher, a man named Tenne. He studied at Drigung under that monastery's second abbot, Gurawa Tsultrim Dorje. (BDRC P4298)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tropu-lotsawa-jampa-pel] Among Tibetans of his day, Tropu Lotsāwa was most famous for building an eighty-cubit-high image of the future Buddha Maitreya, consecrated by Śākyaśrī in 1212. He was one of the significant figures in the early Tropu Kagyu, responsible for bringing the very important Indian Buddhist teachers Mitrayogin, Buddhaśrī, and Śākyaśrī to Tibet. Many of his translations, but only a few of his writings, are available today. (BDRC P4007)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chenga-chokyi-drag] Second Drikung Chungtsang.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chennga-drakpa-jungne] Chennga Drakpa Jungne served nearly two decades as Jikten Gonpo’s personal attendant. [lineage-seed:shangpa-kagyu-lineage:rigong-chokyi-sherab] Fourth holder of the uninterrupted Shangpa golden-doctrine line.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gar-dampa-chodingpa] Śākya Pel, or Gar Dampa Chodingpa, was a disciple of Jikten Gonpo . He founded Choding Monastery and, in the last days of his life, a monastery called Rinchen Ling . His reincarnations are known as the Garchen Rinpoche . (BDRC P813)
[lineage-seed:bodong-lineage:kodrakpa] Received Kalachakra from Vibhuticandra and propagated a distinct Bodong lamdré line.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:kodrakpa-sonam-gyeltsen] Kodrakpa Sonam Gyeltsen is best known as a teacher of the Six Limbed Yoga , the completion process practice of the Kālacakra Tantra . He did not belong to any one particular lineage, although it might be said that he belonged to this particular Kālacakra lineage together with a combination of general Kagyu with the Lamdre lineage of Zhama. (BDRC P1514)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:pajo-drukgom-zhigpo] Pajo Drukgom Zhikpo is a figure of particular importance to Bhutanese history. A layperson, a Drukpa and a disciple of the second abbot of Ralung, he was regarded as a holder of three lineages: Dzogchen, Mahāmudrā of the Drukpa Kagyu, and Zhije. Prophecies guided him to his later career in Bhutan, where he gained considerable political influence. His Drukpa school came into clashes with the Lhapa school, ultimately emerging victorious. This is the reason Bhutan came to be known as “Drukpa Country.” Pajo Drukgom Zhikpo established the first Drukpa monasteries in Bhutan. (BDRC P7852)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lorepa-wangchuk-tsondru] Lorepa is considered the founder of a branch of the Drukpa Kagyu called the Me Druk, or "Lower Druk." A very important teacher during his times, he exemplifies the life of solitary meditation under often difficult circumstances. He founded Tharpaling in Bhutan. (BDRC P4252)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:won-sherab-jungne] Won Sherab Jungne was the compiler and author of the core texts of the Single Intention . A philosophical cycle that revolves around key statements made by Jigten Gonpo , it is still regarded as a one of the main teachings of the Drigung Kagyu lineage. It is for this and for his important biography of his teacher that he is best known today. (BDRC P131)

[lineage-seed:kadam-lineage:tsongkhapa] Received Kadampa lamrim and lojong and founded the Gelug as New Kadampa.
[lineage-seed:zhije-chod-lineage:tsongkhapa-chod] Received Chöd from Shangpa and Zhije masters and integrated it into Gelug practice.
[lineage-seed:ra-luk-lineage:tsongkhapa-yamantaka] Received Ra-line Yamantaka from Rendawa; made it central to Gelug tantric practice.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsongkhapa-lobzang-drakpa] Tsongkhapa Lobzang Drakpa was one of the most influential Tibetan Buddhist scholars of the last millennium. Born in Amdo, he traveled to U-Tsang in his youth, never to return to his homeland. He studied with numerous teachers of all traditions and engaged in many retreats resulting in his development of a fresh interpretation of Nāgārjuna's Madhyamaka view and a reinvigoration of the monastic Vinaya. Widely regarded as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, Tsongkhapa composed eighteen volumes of works of which the majority dealt with tantric subjects. He was the founder of Ganden Monastery, which became the central monastery of the Geluk tradition that was based on his teachings and writings. (BDRC P64)

items.n: The Ninth Taklung Tripa, Tashi Peltsek
items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:taklung-tripa-09-tashi-peltseg] The Ninth Taklung Tripa, Tashi Peltsek, the ninth abbot of Taklung Monastery , lived at a time of great doctinal invention and exchange. He took teachings from masters in all traditions of his day, and, during the more than forty years of his abbacy of Taklung, oversaw an expansion of the monastery and its relations with other institutions. He was granted the title Guoshi from the Yongle Emperor of China the last year of his life. (BDRC P8425)

[lineage-seed:shangpa-kagyu-lineage:tangtong-gyalpo] Shangpa master, iron-bridge builder, and treasure revealer.

[lineage-seed:ra-luk-lineage:gyaltsab-je-yamantaka] First Ganden Tripa; principal heir to Tsongkhapa's Yamantaka teachings.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jamyang-yeshe-rinchen] Jamyang Yeshe Rinchen was the tenth abbot of Ralung Monastery . He was the son of Lodro Sengge and the father of Namkha Pelzang , the eighth and eleventh abbots of Ralung. (BDRC P2632)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:dondrub-gyelpo] Dondrub Gyelpo was the twelfth abbot of Drigung Monastery , from 1395 to 1427. His son from a marriage prior to his ordination succeeded him as abbot. (BDRC P503)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drungchen-khachopa-namkha-gyeltsen] A prince of a ruling family of Markham, Drungchen Khachopa Namkha Gyeltsen studied with lamas of all the major traditions, founding a monastery in the Dzachu River Valley north of Chamdo called Namgyel Gang. As ruler of a petty kingdom he had an audience with the Yongle Emperor of the Ming Dynasty. He passed away at Emei Shan in Sichuan. (BDRC P4086)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:duldzin-drakpa-gyeltsen] Duldzin Drakpa Gyeltsen was one of the principle disciples of Tsongkhapa and Gyeltsab Je. He was famed for his writing on the Vinaya, some of which are included in traditional Geluk monastic education. (BDRC P1591)
[lineage-seed:bodong-lineage:chokle-namgyel] Greatest Bodong master; encyclopedic scholar and institutional founder of the tradition.
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tashi-pelden] Jamyang Choje Tashi Pelden, a close disciple of Tsongkhapa , founded Drepung Monastery in 1416. He composed the Secret Biography of Tsongkhapa. (BDRC P35)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chennga-sonam-zangpo] Chennga Sonam Zangpo was an abbot of Densatil Monastery and a student of Tsongkhapa , whom he encouraged to write the Ngakrim Chenmo. (BDRC P1AG39)

[rigpa-wiki:Ngorchen Kunga Zangpo] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:ngorchen-kunga-zangpo] Texts by and about Ngorchen Kunga Zangpo (ngor chen kun dga' bzang po, 1382–1456), one of the most prolific and influential masters in the Sakya school and the founder of Ngor Monastery:
[lineage-seed:lamdre-lineage:ngorchen-kunga-zangpo] Founder of Ngor; absorbed Bodong lamdré and codified the path-and-result cycles.
[lineage-seed:bodong-lineage:sherab-sengge] Disciple of Bodong Panchen; maintained the Bodong scholastic seat.
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:karmapa-v] Fifth Karmapa; imperial teacher in China.

[rigpa-wiki:Vanaratna] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:vanaratna] Vanaratna was a Bengali Tantric Buddhist master known in Tibet as "the last Indian paṇḍita." He traveled in Tibet three times in the first half of the thirteenth century. A master of the Kālacakra, he was a preceptor to some of the last heads of Pakmodru family, and enjoyed patronage from the members of the Rinpung family in Shigatse. Among his disciples were Rongton Sheja Kunrik , Go Lotsawa Zhonnu Pel , and Trimkhang Lotsāwa Sonam Gyatso ; the second of these students composed a biography, which was completed by the third. (BDRC P207)

[rigpa-wiki:Lama Khedrup] [rigpa-wiki:Khedrup Gyatso] [rigpa-wiki:Khedrup Gelek Palzang] [rigpa-wiki:Khedrup Do-ngak Tendzin] [lineage-seed:gelug-lineage:khedrup-je] Disciple of Tsongkhapa; Guhyasamaja commentator.
[lineage-seed:kadam-lineage:khedrup-je] Disciple of Tsongkhapa who systematized Gelug scholasticism.
[lineage-seed:ra-luk-lineage:khedrup-je-yamantaka] Author of major Yamantaka commentaries in the Gelug tradition.
[lineage-seed:gelug-lineage:dalai-lama-i] Posthumously first Dalai Lama.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:go-lotsawa-zhonnu-pel] Go Lotsāwa Zhonnu Pel was the author of the important Tibetan history The Blue Annals . A Kagyu polymath, he studied under some sixty prominent lamas, chief among them the Fifth Karmapa Dezhin Shekpa . He was a Sanskrit scholar and served as translator to an Indian scholar Paṇḍit Vanaratna for five years. He was a teacher of the Seventh Karmapa, Chodrak Gyatso , and the Fourth Zhamar, Chodrak Yeshe . (BDRC P318)

[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:go-lotsawa-zhonnu-pal] Texts by and about Gö Lotsāwa Zhönnu Pal ('gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal, 1392–1481), author of the famous history The Blue Annals (deb ther sngon po):

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jangsem-sherab-zangpo] Jangsem Sherab Zangpo, a disciple of Tsongkhapa , founded the great Geluk monastery of Chamdo Chokhor Jampa Ling in 1437. Prior to meeting Tsongkhapa he had trained in many traditions, including the Karma Kagyu, Jonang, and Sakya. (BDRC P2CZ9156)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rinchen-wanggyel] Rinchen Wanggyel was the thirteenth abbot of Drigung Monastery . He was the son of the twelfth abbot, Dondrub Gyelpo and served the office of Drigung Gompo before ordaining. According to legend he left office for  Wutai Shan  in China, where over the next few centuries he occasionally appeared to visiting Drigung lamas. (BDRC P4589)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drukchen-02-kunga-peljor] The Second Drukchen, Kunga Peljor, was the thirteenth abbot of Ralung Monastery . He was the son of Sherab Zangpo who was the twelfth abbot of Ralung. He was identified as the reincarnation of Tsangpa Gyare , the founder of the Drukpa tradition. Kunga Peljor also served as abbot of Daklha Gampo . (BDRC P920)

He restored the temple at  Sekhar Gutok , the site of Milarepa 's tower, and made it the base for his religious activities. (BDRC P818)

items.n: The Second Tai Situ, Tashi Namgyel
items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:second-tai-situ-tashi-namgyel] Tashi Namgyel, the Second Tai Situ, was recognized by the Sixth Karmapa . Little is currently known about his life. (BDRC P820)

[rigpa-wiki:Tsangnyön Heruka] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsangnyon-heruka] Perhaps best known today as the author and publisher of the famous biography and collected songs of Milarepa, Tsangnyon Heruka was also one of the most influential mad yogins of Tibet. He is famous for having renovated the Svayambhū Stūpa in the Kathmandu Valley, and for inspiring a whole school of textual production and printing, sometimes referred to as “the School of Tsangnyon.” Tsangnyon practiced and disseminated the core teachings of the Kagyu tradition: the Six Dharmas of Nāropa, Mahāmudrā, and the Aural Transmissions that had been transmitted by Milarepa’s closest disciples. (BDRC P442)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:karmapa-vii] Seventh Karmapa; author of Ocean of Reasoning.

items.n: The First Sanggye Nyenpa, Tashi Peljor
items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sanggye-nyenpa-tashi-peljor] Sanggye Nyenpa was a student of the Seventh Karmapa and one of the four main teachers of the Eighth Karmapa , who composed several biographies about him. (BDRC P1012)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:unyon-kunga-zangpo] Kunga Zangpo, popularly known as the Madman of U, was one of central Tibet's famous "mad yogis" of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. Trained as a monk, he shed his robes for the ornate costume of an Indian siddha and attracted disciples from across central Tibet. (BDRC P814)
